title: WordPress Contact Form Not Sending Email? A Step-by-Step Diagnosis
meta_title: WordPress Form Not Sending Email? Diagnosis Checklist
meta_desc: Trace a WordPress enquiry from form submission to storage, sending and inbox delivery. Diagnose recipient settings, SMTP tests and confirmation messages.
excerpt: Trace a WordPress enquiry from form submission to storage, sending and inbox delivery. Diagnose recipient settings, SMTP tests and confirmation messages.
content:
Quick Answer

Test the real form and follow one labelled enquiry through validation, storage, sending and the recipient inbox. A success message or a successful mail-function result does not prove inbox delivery. Identify the failed stage before changing plugins or requesting a redesign.

The First Question: What Exactly Is Missing?

“The contact form is not working” can describe several different failures. The button might do nothing, the form might reject valid details, the request might save without sending a notification, or the email might reach a mailbox that nobody checks. Start by describing the symptom precisely.

Write down the page, the form, the time of the test and the message shown to the visitor. Agree a test with the person receiving notifications and use clearly labelled sample details. One identifiable test is easier to investigate than repeated submissions scattered across several forms.

This guide explains a troubleshooting sequence for a WordPress website. Storage and logging depend on the installed form system; do not assume every plugin keeps submissions. If a form is already losing enquiries, give visitors a working alternative contact route while the underlying issue is investigated.

1. Follow One Enquiry Through Four Separate Stages

Think of the request as four stages: the browser sends it, the application accepts it, the notification system processes it and the recipient can find it. A failure at one stage should be investigated there rather than treated as proof that the entire website needs replacing.

The WordPress wp_mail documentation explicitly distinguishes a successful function result from a recipient receiving the email. That is why a successful mail test must be paired with an actual inbox check.

For an illustrative test, label the message “Website delivery test 16 October” and record the time. Check the expected entry store, if your form has one, and match the same test to sending logs and the recipient mailbox. This is an example process, not a claim that our team has tested your particular website.

Observed symptomWhat it establishesNext inspection
Click produces no visible responseThe visitor cannot complete the normal pathBrowser validation and request errors
Success message, no stored entryThe interface reported success; storage is unconfirmedWhether this form stores entries and whether the handler completed
Stored entry, sending errorThe application received the enquiryNotification configuration and transport logs
Sending accepted, inbox emptyThe sending system processed or accepted the requestDelivery events, spam folders and mailbox rules
Email arrives, nobody repliesDelivery may be workingOwnership and follow-up workflow

2. Test the Actual Page, Not Only a Plugin Test Button

Open the public page as a normal visitor. Check the form on a phone and on a desktop, including any consent or anti-spam step that applies. A test from a plugin settings screen can use a different recipient or template from the form customers actually submit.

Try a valid enquiry, a missing required value and an invalid email address. The form should explain corrections clearly and avoid claiming success after a failed request. Inspect the actual result before repeatedly clicking the button; duplicate attempts can make the evidence harder to follow.

If the problem appeared after an update, record which plugin, theme or server changes occurred around that time. Investigate in a staging environment where possible. Turning off every plugin on a business website can disrupt unrelated features and makes it difficult to identify which change mattered.

3. Check Where Entries Are Supposed to Be Stored

Ask whether your form system stores submissions, and where authorised staff should find them. Some installations rely on notifications; others include an entry inbox or a separate storage integration. Verify the installed configuration instead of assuming an admin menu exists.

If storage is configured, compare the test timestamp and service information with the record. Check that the page attribution and contact method are present. A record missing its email address is a different problem from a complete record whose notification was not delivered.

If the business needs an enquiry history, include that requirement explicitly in the repair scope. Decide who can access it, how long it should be kept and how staff recover requests when email is unavailable. Avoid storing unnecessary personal information merely because a plugin offers more fields.

4. Inspect Recipient, Sender and Reply-To Separately

Check the real destination address for each public form. An old staff mailbox, an incorrect service-routing rule or a mistyped address can make a valid enquiry appear lost. Do not assume every form uses the same recipient as the main contact page.

For Contact Form 7, its official mail setup documentation explains the To and From fields and additional headers. It specifies a same-domain sender for that plugin’s configuration. Follow the form system and mail provider’s instructions rather than placing the visitor’s address into every header.

Keep the purpose of each field clear. The destination receives the notification; the sending identity must fit the configured service; the reply route should let staff answer the visitor appropriately. Ask the developer to show a labelled test message and verify that clicking Reply produces the intended recipient.

5. Use SMTP Evidence to Narrow the Problem

An authenticated sending service can provide a clearer transport configuration and useful delivery records, but installing an SMTP plugin is not a complete diagnosis. Identify which service is active, who owns the account and whether its credentials and sending configuration are still valid.

Run the service’s approved test, then repeat the actual public form. If the service test arrives but the form notification does not, compare their recipients, sender identities, templates and routing rules. That difference is valuable evidence; changing providers immediately may hide it.

If the transport test fails, record the error and ask the host or sending provider to investigate the relevant connection or account issue. Do not publish credentials in screenshots or support posts. Have the responsible provider confirm any domain-authentication requirements and configuration changes for the chosen sending route.

6. Distinguish Acceptance from Inbox Delivery

Inspect the sending provider’s delivery record where available. A request accepted for processing, a delivered message and a bounced message are different outcomes. Match the record to the labelled test instead of interpreting an unrelated email event as confirmation.

Ask the recipient to check spam, quarantine, mailbox forwarding and rules. Check whether the address is a shared inbox with access or routing restrictions. A second agreed destination can help narrow the problem, but successful delivery there still does not prove delivery to the original mailbox.

When reporting the repair, state the evidence precisely: the form saved the test; the sender accepted it; the intended recipient located it. Keep any stage that remains unverified visible in the handover. This avoids calling a repair complete merely because the website displayed a green message.

7. Review the Visitor’s Error and Success States

A visitor should understand whether the enquiry was received and what happens next. Use a clear confirmation based on the application’s actual result. If email notifications are temporarily unavailable but the request was reliably stored, the business should decide how that outcome is communicated and handled.

The W3C form notification guidance covers understandable error and success feedback. Include missing fields, invalid details and server failures in the acceptance checklist. Verify that a visitor can locate the correction and retry without losing useful input.

Provide an accurate alternative such as an email address or a contact link the business monitors. Keep the message helpful rather than displaying internal stack traces. An alternative contact method is useful during recovery, but the original form still needs a defined repair owner.

8. Verify the Fix with a Small Test Matrix

A single successful submission can miss differences between forms or contact methods. List the important public forms and test the supported routes after the fix. Check mobile and desktop behaviour, required-field validation, storage if configured and the intended notification recipient.

Use synthetic details and coordinate the tests so staff do not mistake them for new prospects. Record the time and result without copying personal enquiry content into general analytics or public tickets. Keep any test records clearly distinguished from genuine lead reports.

After a relevant plugin, hosting or mail-service change, repeat the small acceptance set. This is a practical maintenance task, not a promise that no future delivery problem can occur. Choose a review frequency based on how important the enquiry route is to the business.

Test casePass condition
Valid enquiry on the main formExpected record and notification verified
Alternative supported contact methodDetails retained and correctly routed
Invalid or missing detailsClear correction; no false success
Secondary service formCorrect service recipient and page attribution
Temporary submission failureHelpful message and usable retry route

What to Send When Asking for Help

Send the affected URL, form plugin and version, approximate time the issue began, the exact visitor message and the stages already checked. Share the labelled test outcome through the agreed support channel. Keep credentials and customer information out of the initial brief.

Ask the scope to cover diagnosis, the actual repair, end-to-end verification and a short handover. A proposal to install another plugin without identifying the failed stage may leave the same uncertainty. For the broader customer journey, see our website lead audit guide.

If you need help investigating the WordPress implementation, explore our WordPress development services or send the affected page and symptoms through our project enquiry page. We can define the work around the evidence available, without pretending that email delivery has been verified before testing.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why does the form show success when no email arrives?

The interface, entry storage and notification delivery are separate stages. A success message may describe the form handler’s result without proving that the intended recipient received the notification. Trace one labelled test through the configured stages.

Does wp_mail returning true prove inbox delivery?

No. WordPress documents that a true result does not automatically mean the recipient received the message. Confirm the sending record and the actual destination mailbox separately.

Will an SMTP plugin automatically solve the problem?

Not necessarily. It can configure a sending route, but incorrect recipients, form-specific templates, invalid credentials or mailbox filtering may still need investigation. Test both the transport and the public form.

Does every WordPress contact form store entries?

No assumption should be made. Storage depends on the plugin and configuration. Verify the installed system and explicitly scope an enquiry history if the business needs one.

title: Shopify Product Page Audit: What to Fix Before Changing Your Theme
meta_title: Shopify Product Page Audit: Images, Variants & Mobile
meta_desc: Audit Shopify product pages before changing themes. Check images, variants, fulfilment details, cart behaviour, mobile layouts and meaningful sales measurements.
excerpt: Audit Shopify product pages before changing themes. Check images, variants, fulfilment details, cart behaviour, mobile layouts and meaningful sales measurements.
content:
Quick Answer

Audit a representative product page before changing the whole theme. Check whether customers understand the item, choose the correct variant, see fulfilment information and recover from errors on mobile. Compare those findings with the actual customer journey before deciding what to redesign.

Start with a Product Decision, Not a Theme Demo

A store owner may see visitors leaving a product page and assume the design needs replacing. Sometimes the problem is visual hierarchy; sometimes it is an unclear size, a missing image, unavailable stock or an unexpected delivery condition. A new theme does not automatically resolve incomplete product information.

Choose a product that represents a commercially important journey. Include one item with options and one with a known customer question. Review the page from arrival through selection, cart and the relevant checkout steps. Use observed problems to define the work.

This is a practical Shopify product-page audit framework, not a claim that a particular layout will produce a fixed conversion lift. The examples are illustrative. Their purpose is to help the store team distinguish content, configuration and development problems before paying for a broader redesign.

1. Write Down What the Customer Must Understand

List the facts a buyer needs before choosing the product. Depending on the item, that may include dimensions, materials, compatibility, fit, package contents, care requirements or production time. Check that the published description answers those questions accurately.

Start with questions received by support or sales. An anonymised pattern such as “customers ask whether the adapter fits their model” can reveal a missing compatibility section. A longer paragraph of promotional copy may not answer that question as well as a clear specification or example.

Give each fact a content owner. The design team should not invent specifications, promises or fulfilment details to complete the layout. Agree which information is available now and which needs business approval before publication.

2. Check Images Against the Buying Questions

Review what each image contributes. One might explain the product’s overall appearance, another its scale and another a detail customers commonly ask about. Several nearly identical images can take space without helping a decision.

Shopify’s product media documentation describes supported product-media options. Choose the media that serves the item and the team’s publishing workflow. Do not assume every product needs video or a complex viewer to be understandable.

On mobile, inspect the first image, gallery navigation, cropping and detail readability. Check that useful information is also available as text rather than embedded only in a promotional graphic. Use authorised images that represent the actual product, and record who will maintain them when the catalogue changes.

3. Make the Selected Variant Unambiguous

A customer should understand which size, finish, colour or configuration they are choosing. The selected option should be clear, and relevant availability and product information should remain consistent with that selection. Inspect the actual combinations instead of testing only the default item.

The Shopify variants guide explains options and combinations of option values. For your audit, list the combinations that need a different SKU, stock record, price or media treatment. Then verify the configured behaviour on the storefront.

Use an illustrative example: a lamp sold in two finishes and two sizes. Check all supported combinations, including any unavailable one. Confirm that the cart contains the chosen size and finish. This sample helps define acceptance tests; it is not a statement about your current store’s catalogue.

QuestionWhat to inspectEvidence to record
What am I buying?Specification and included itemsThe page answers the priority customer questions
Which option is selected?Size, finish or configuration controlsSelected option and cart line agree
Is this available?Stock and made-to-order messagingAvailability matches the selected combination
What happens after purchase?Dispatch, delivery or collection detailsRelevant expectations appear before commitment
Can I correct a mistake?Errors and cart editingThe visitor can understand and recover

4. Put Fulfilment Information Near the Decision

Identify what customers need to know about dispatch, delivery, collection or made-to-order work before adding the item. The store’s operational owner should approve the wording and rules. Avoid a reassuring sentence that conflicts with the actual checkout configuration.

Check whether the message changes for different products or options. A stock item and a custom configuration may have different lead times. If a destination affects availability or shipping choices, make the relevant conditions understandable without publishing an unverified promise.

Review the route to detailed policies, but do not make a visitor search through a long policy page for an essential product fact. Summarise the relevant point accurately and provide a clear route to the full information. Have the business review policy wording and operational assumptions.

5. Inspect the Add-to-Cart and Error Journey

Check the action itself: selected variant, quantity, availability and the cart result. The button should not leave the visitor wondering whether the action completed. If there is a loading state or an error, the page should communicate it in a useful place.

Test an unavailable combination and a quantity that cannot be fulfilled. Inspect any relevant limits, custom fields or purchase options. A visually attractive button is not enough when the underlying rules produce the wrong item or an unclear rejection.

Review keyboard use and visible labels on interactive controls. Where an error is presented, the visitor should know what needs changing and how to continue. Include a realistic error state in the design discussion rather than approving only the ideal purchase flow.

6. Test the Whole Mobile Page with Real Content

Open the page on a phone with the actual product name, images, option values and delivery notes. Inspect what the customer sees before the main action and what requires excessive scrolling. Long names or multiple option groups often expose weaknesses hidden by demonstration content.

Check tap targets, gallery controls and any sticky purchase bar. A sticky action should preserve the meaning of the selected item and avoid covering important content. Treat it as an interaction to test, not a feature to add merely because another store uses one.

Review overlays such as chat, newsletter prompts and app widgets together. Each may work independently while their combined placement blocks product details or controls. Record the conflict and the affected screen width so the repair is specific.

7. Check the App and Performance Trade-Offs

List the apps and embedded tools that affect the product page. For each, identify its purpose, owner and the customer problem it solves. Reviews, recommendations, chat and promotional tools should have a defined role rather than being added without a maintenance decision.

If the page feels slow, inspect representative pages and devices before assigning a cause. Large media, scripts, widgets and theme behaviour can interact. Ask for evidence of the affected journey and the proposed change instead of assuming every delay requires a new theme.

Test changes in an appropriate preview or staging workflow. Removing an app or switching a theme can affect functionality beyond the selected product. Agree the comparison and rollback path with the responsible developer, then repeat the important product and cart checks.

8. Measure Outcomes at the Correct Stage

Separate product views, option interactions, add-to-cart actions, checkout starts and confirmed purchases. These stages answer different questions. A product-page change cannot be evaluated fairly if the reporting treats a click as a paid order.

Review device, traffic source and product context where the data supports it. A campaign bringing the wrong audience may produce a different pattern from a confusing variant selector. Small samples and changes in promotions or availability can also make comparisons unreliable.

Keep a short change log: issue, hypothesis, proposed repair, date and acceptance result. Change one coherent part of the journey at a time where practical. Do not label an observation as proof of a guaranteed conversion improvement.

9. Decide Between Content Repair, Template Work and Redesign

Classify what the audit found. Missing specifications and unclear images may need content work. Incorrect options or inventory may need catalogue configuration. Broken controls or unsuitable layout may need template development. A broader redesign becomes easier to scope once those problems are understood.

Ask a proposal to state which product templates, apps, data changes and tests are included. Decide who supplies approved copy and media, who checks option behaviour and who signs off the launch. Keep recurring app costs and maintenance responsibilities visible.

For a wider store project, our ecommerce website brief checklist covers catalogue, integrations and launch planning. You can also review our Shopify development and ecommerce website services.

A Useful Brief for Your First Audit Discussion

Send the store URL, a few representative product links, the main customer complaint or drop-off concern and any known configuration issues. Include the important apps, the content owner and the relevant analytics definitions. Use anonymised examples when sharing support patterns.

Ask for a prioritised issue list and acceptance checks before committing to extensive work. The team should be able to explain why each repair matters to a customer task and how the corrected behaviour will be verified. That makes the discussion more useful than a generic instruction to modernise the site.

If you need help reviewing the product journey, send the example pages through our project enquiry page. We can scope content, template or development work around the observed problems without promising a particular sales result.

Frequently Asked Questions

Should I change my Shopify theme if product pages are not converting?

Audit the journey first. Content, variant configuration, stock, fulfilment information, traffic quality and implementation can all affect the result. A theme change should address identified requirements.

Which product pages should I test first?

Choose commercially important and representative items, including a product with options and one that generates repeated customer questions. Add edge cases such as unavailable combinations.

What should happen when a variant changes?

The selected option should remain clear, related information should be consistent, and the cart should contain the intended combination. Test the configured behaviour for your catalogue rather than assuming it works.

Can a product-page audit guarantee more sales?

No. It identifies issues and priorities that can be checked and measured. Sales also depend on audience, demand, product fit, pricing, availability and other factors outside the page layout.
